Amine Laabi considère qu’il a beaucoup d: Amine Laabi considers himself very lucky. Not because he managed to make it thanks to his passion – cooking – but because it allowed him to bring his people together and inspire his community.
C’est d’ailleurs dans le cadre d’une act: It was during a joint activity by the Centre Binetna and the Forum jeunesse de Saint-Michel, which we took part in, that he cooked an iftar (the meal that breaks the fast during the month of Ramadan) with about twenty young Montrealers. All day long, he guided the teens and taught them the culinary arts, chatting and joking with them throughout the whole preparation.
Derrière les fourneaux, Amine est un pro: Behind the stove, Amine is a pro, but with his good humour and empathy, he constantly reminds us that everything he does for teens comes from his own experience growing up in a Montréal neighbourhood.

« J’ai vu beaucoup de violence très jeun: “I saw a lot of violence very young. I wasn’t drawn to it, but I wasn’t an angel either…” That is how the Montréal chef answers when asked to describe what makes the neighbourhood he grew up in what it is.
Nous sommes samedi en fin d’après-midi,: It’s Saturday late afternoon, and Amine has just finished cooking tonight’s meal with about ten young people. A little out of breath, he takes the time to sit down and collect his thoughts so he can walk us through his life story.
Amine est né au Maroc, puis sa famille a: Amine was born in Morocco, then his family immigrated and settled in the Saint-Laurent borough, in the northwest of the city. At 11, he discovered a new country, a new language, a new neighbourhood. “I wasn’t good at school,” he says, laughing. “Actually, I hated school. I had an attention disorder that wasn’t diagnosed at the time. It was really hard for me to succeed or to enjoy learning when I didn’t understand why I was struggling,” he adds.
Selon lui, il a le « parcours typique d’: By his own account, he has the “typical path of a guy from Ville Saint-Laurent.” Yet he is about to transform that stereotype and show that “coming from here isn’t something to be ashamed of, it’s something to be proud of.”
S’il travaillait dur pour s’en sortir, m: Even as he worked hard to get by, sometimes juggling multiple jobs and stretching his hours, Amine remained a motivated young man among friends and acquaintances who tended to give in to disillusionment. “A lot of the guys I hung out with as a teenager ended up in prison and regretted trying to make it through dishonest means. Some of my friends also lost their lives,” he says thoughtfully. “It made me think a lot, and I realized it wasn’t too late for me to make it without going down that road.”
Amine a donc dû « tout faire pour sa pas: So Amine had to “do everything for his passion.” Today, the wave of love and support he receives on social media and in life in general reminds him that his hard work was not in vain. “I’m a community guy, it always makes me happy and warms my heart when I see guys from the hood appreciate what I do,” he says.

Étant arrivé à Montréal à un jeune âge,: Having arrived in Montréal at a young age, Amine comes from an immigrant background and sees himself in the racialized youth affected by the problem of violence in their neighbourhoods.
« Ça me fait vraiment mal au cœur de voi: “It really breaks my heart to see young people from my community involved in violent stuff. I hear stories of violence worthy of a movie, too intense for me to believe they’re real,” says the cook, astonished. “A lot of them left their jobs and their lives elsewhere to live a worse life here. I think a lot of young people don’t realize how much their parents fought and sacrificed for them.”
Il constate aussi que les personnes raci: He also observes that there aren’t that many racialized people who serve as role models for young people. “When I was young, there was only Rachid Badouri I could identify with. I would see him on TV and tell myself that I could get there one day if he had made it. Today, I hope I’m doing that, and when I get messages from young people telling me they were inspired by me, it’s a real source of pride,” he says with an enormous smile.
« Je te garantis que, parmi tous ceux qu: “I guarantee you that among everyone who chose the path of crime, not one has made it,” says Amine. It’s what he never tires of repeating to the youngest people in his neighbourhood: “You’ll end up either dead or in prison.”
Il insiste sur la nécessité de tenir les: He stresses the need to keep teenagers busy: “Young people need to develop passions; you have to sign them up for sports, for activities, whatever. If a young person is busy doing something they love, I think they’re much less likely to end up in street gangs or in something else tied to violence.”
Le chef insiste aussi sur l’importance d: The chef also emphasizes the importance of thinking about your future when you’re young. While it’s easy for teens to be influenced and to be carefree, he believes they must believe in themselves and in what they love to do. “If you’re determined and you want to work, you’re definitely going to succeed in the long run. It’s way better than doing stupid stuff, and that’s for sure,” says the cordon bleu cook, addressing his message to young people.
Plus de 15 ans après avoir quitté l’écol: More than 15 years after leaving high school, the chef received some news. Recently, he was contacted by his former school, Émile-Legault, in Saint-Laurent, which invited him to come talk to students about his journey.
Mine de rien, cette invitation a grandem: Without making a big deal of it, the invitation deeply moved the cook. “It really did something to me,” he says quietly. “It’s not a school with a very good reputation, and when they asked me to come speak, I felt like I was in the shoes of the students there, who didn’t really have any resources.”
« Être pris comme exemple pour prouver a: “Being used as an example to prove to young people in Saint-Laurent that it’s possible to succeed, even if you come from the neighbourhood, it moved me,” he adds, with stars in his eyes.
« Tout ce que je savais, quand j’étais j: “All I knew when I was young was that I liked to eat,” he says, laughing. He goes on to confide that cooking is what saved him professionally, but also in life. “Of course, it opened a lot of doors for me, but it’s also what kept me a bit away from trouble. I had a passion, a goal, and when you have those two ingredients when you’re young, it guides you a lot,” he concludes.
Le Montréalais, aujourd’hui âgé de 31 an: The Montrealer, now 31, left school in his 3<sup>rd</sup> year of high school, lacking motivation and struggling academically. He started working early on to make a living. “At 18, I found myself with a lot of responsibilities. I’d moved out of my parents’ place with my brother, and I had to find a way to pay my rent and my bills,” he recalls.
Après presque une décennie à travailler: After nearly a decade working in sales, he felt ready to move up the ladder. Yet the food lover was already thinking about enrolling in cooking school. But everything seemed to suggest it wasn’t the right path: he would have to quit his job and start over from scratch, with no guarantee of success. “It was a real headache. Since I’d left school in my 3<sup>rd</sup> year of high school, I had to get my academic equivalencies before I could get into cooking school. I had to figure it out on my own,” he says.
